tool.name: LandformClassification
tool.summary: Classifies a DEM into landform categories (canyons, valleys, plains, open and upper slopes, ridges, peaks) from a small- and a large-neighborhood Topographic Position Index (TPI) plus slope, using a saved classification system such as the Weiss 10-class. The two TPIs and slope are computed internally (no Spatial Analyst extension), or you may supply pre-computed rasters.
tool.usage:
Landform classification combines the Topographic Position Index (TPI = a cell's elevation minus the mean elevation of a neighborhood around it; Weiss 2001) at two scales -- a small and a large neighborhood -- plus slope. The combination is what distinguishes landforms: a cell that is high relative to its immediate surroundings but low relative to the broad landscape is a local ridge or hill within a larger valley, while low-small plus high-large is an upland drainage. With two TPI scales and slope you can separate canyons, midslope drainages, U-shaped valleys, plains, open slopes, upper slopes and mesas, local and midslope ridges, and mountain tops.
The two neighborhoods set the two scales, and choosing them is the crux of the analysis. TPI is inherently scale-dependent -- the same point can read as a valley at one scale and a hilltop at another, both valid -- so the small neighborhood should capture the local features you care about and the large neighborhood the broad context. Radius may be in cells or ground units (meters, feet, ...), as a circle (all cells within the radius) or an annulus (a ring between an inner and outer radius; Weiss's own examples used annuli). The neighborhoods are computed exactly, avoiding the cell-rounding quirks of some focal-statistics tools.
Raw versus standardized TPI -- primarily a property of the classification system, and when computing on-the-fly also the two TPI-type dropdowns on this dialog (one per neighborhood scale, each defaulting to what the system expects for that scale; the two may differ, so a classification can combine, say, a raw small-neighborhood TPI with a percentile large-neighborhood TPI). Raw TPI (elevation units) is absolute: a 100 m hill reads the same everywhere, usually the better fit for ecological and wildlife questions. Standardized TPI is relative to variability (whole-raster, or the neighborhood for the SD units), so a small bump on a plain and a large hill in the mountains can share a class -- good for cross-landscape comparison but potentially misleading ecologically. Weiss's 10-class default uses standardized units. Edit the units, thresholds, names, and colors in the Classification System Builder.
Classification systems are reusable, named JSON rule sets stored in a per-user location that survives add-in reinstalls; this tool lists the landform systems it finds (the bundled default is Weiss's 10-class). Classification is applied cell-by-cell in one vectorized pass -- each class is the AND of its criteria across the two TPIs and slope, and where classes overlap the lowest class value wins -- with no Esri Con or Spatial Analyst. Per-class colors symbolize the output when it is added to the map.
References: Weiss, A. 2001. Topographic Position and Landforms Analysis. ESRI International User Conference poster. Guisan, A., S. B. Weiss, and A. D. Weiss. 1999. Plant Ecology 143:107-122 (https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1009841519580). Jenness, J. 2006. Topographic Position Index (tpi_jen.avx) extension for ArcView 3.x (http://www.jennessent.com/arcview/tpi.htm).

dialogReference.para: Choose how the tool obtains the two TPIs and slope it classifies:

Calculate TPI and Slope on-the-fly from DEM (default) -- both TPIs (small and large neighborhood) and slope are computed from an input DEM using the settings below. Only the "Calculate on-the-fly (from DEM)" parameters apply.
Use Existing TPI and Slope Rasters -- the tool classifies small-TPI, large-TPI, and slope rasters you already have. Only the "Use existing rasters" parameters apply; the DEM is not needed.
The tool classifies whatever values it is given as-is; the classification system's units are used only to warn about a possible mismatch, and the tool always still runs.

The elevation raster (DEM), single band -- required when calculating on-the-fly; ignored (and greyed out) when using existing rasters. Projected and geographic coordinate systems are both supported (geographic distances handled per row on the spheroid, so a ground-unit radius changes with Latitude in order to maintain a true circle on the ground).

The saved landform classification system to apply. The list is read from the per-user store; the bundled default is the Weiss 10-class landform system. Author new systems with the Classification System Builder. When you pick a system, the on-the-fly TPI-type and slope-units dropdowns default to what it expects (you may override them).

The output integer landform raster, carrying a Value / Class_Name attribute table and a color map from the classification system (including any per-class opacity, so e.g. a hillshade can show through selected classes). Cells matching no class (or outside the data) are unclassified. Any unit-compatibility warnings are also written to the output's metadata. A name is suggested from the input.
Circle or Annulus for the small-scale TPI neighborhood. On-the-fly only.
The (outer) radius of the small neighborhood -- the local scale. Larger values blur out the finest features. On-the-fly only.
Inner radius of the small annulus (ignored for a circle). On-the-fly only.
Cells or a ground unit (Meters, Kilometers, Feet, Miles) for the small-neighborhood radius. A ground-unit radius is converted to a number of cells using the DEM's cell size. On-the-fly only.

On a geographic (latitude/longitude) DEM the cell size in meters is worked out separately for the east-west (width) and north-south (height) directions -- the east-west width is computed per row on the spheroid and shrinks toward the poles, while the north-south height is essentially constant -- and the radius is converted to a cell count on each axis independently. This produces an elliptical kernel in pixel space that is a true circle on the ground; and because the east-west width changes with Latitude, the horizontal radius (in cells) is recomputed row by row, so the neighborhood stays a true circle on the ground at every latitude.
Circle or Annulus for the large-scale TPI neighborhood. On-the-fly only.

The (outer) radius of the large neighborhood -- the broad context scale. Make it clearly larger than the small radius so the two capture different landform scales; the tool warns if it is not (when the two radii are in comparable units). On-the-fly only.
Inner radius of the large annulus (ignored for a circle). On-the-fly only.

Cells or a ground unit (Meters, Kilometers, Feet, Miles) for the large-neighborhood radius. A ground-unit radius is converted to cells using the DEM's cell size; on a geographic (latitude/longitude) DEM the cell width in meters is computed per row on the spheroid and the radius is sized on each axis so the neighborhood is a true circle on the ground, recomputed row by row so it stays a true circle at every latitude (see the small-neighborhood radius units for the full explanation). On-the-fly only.

Which form of TPI to compute from the DEM for the small neighborhood, when calculating on-the-fly: Raw (elevation units), Neighborhood standard deviation (the raw TPI over the neighborhood SD of elevation, Weiss's standardized form), or Percentile. The small and large neighborhoods choose their TPI types independently, so a classification may combine different types at the two scales. This defaults to the form the selected classification system expects for its small-neighborhood TPI, but you may change it; if it does not match the system's units the tool warns and still runs. (The whole-raster DEM-scale standardized form is intentionally not offered here, because it tracks absolute elevation rather than neighborhood position.)

Which form of TPI to compute from the DEM for the large neighborhood, when calculating on-the-fly: Raw (elevation units), Neighborhood standard deviation, or Percentile. Chosen independently of the small-neighborhood TPI type, so a classification may combine different types at the two scales. Defaults to the form the selected classification system expects for its large-neighborhood TPI; if it does not match the system's units the tool warns and still runs.
The DEM's elevation units (Meters or Feet), for the slope calculation. Detected and locked when the DEM defines a vertical coordinate system. On-the-fly only.
Planar (default) or Geodesic slope for a projected DEM; geographic DEMs are always geodesic. On-the-fly only.

Compute slope in Degrees or Percent rise, when calculating on-the-fly. Defaults to the units the selected system's slope thresholds assume; if you choose the other units the tool warns and still runs. The chosen units are stamped into any saved slope raster. On-the-fly only.
Optional. When calculating on-the-fly, save the generated small-neighborhood TPI raster here (stamped with its TPI type). Leave blank to keep it in memory only. On-the-fly only.
Optional. When calculating on-the-fly, save the generated large-neighborhood TPI raster here (stamped with its TPI type). Leave blank to keep it in memory only. On-the-fly only.
Optional. When calculating on-the-fly, save the generated slope raster here (stamped with its slope units). Leave blank to keep it in memory only. On-the-fly only.

The pre-computed small-neighborhood TPI raster to classify, when using existing rasters (must match the other rasters' extent and cell size). Its values are classified as-is; its TPI type is read from its metadata if present, otherwise declare it in the dropdown below this parameter.

Rasters made by the Topographic Position Index tool (or saved by this tool) also record their neighborhood radius in their metadata, and the tool warns if this "small" TPI's radius is not smaller than the "large" TPI's -- swapped or duplicated inputs would silently produce a wrong classification. Rasters made by other software, or by these tools before the radius stamp was added, cannot be checked.

param.name: declare_tpi_type_small
param.displayname: Declare small-neighborhood TPI type (optional, for warnings)

dialogReference.para: Optional. Declare what kind of TPI the existing small-neighborhood raster holds (Raw, Neighborhood standard deviation, DEM-scale standard deviation, or Percentile) when it is not stamped in the raster's metadata. The small and large TPIs are declared independently, so a classification may combine different TPI types at the two scales. Used only to warn about possibly incompatible units; the tool still runs even if a warning is shown. Leave blank if you do not want to declare it.

The pre-computed large-neighborhood TPI raster to classify, when using existing rasters (must match the other rasters' extent and cell size). Classified as-is; its TPI type is read from its metadata if present, otherwise declare it in the dropdown below this parameter. Its neighborhood radius is also read from its metadata when our TPI tools recorded it, and the tool warns if it is not larger than the small-neighborhood TPI's radius (see the small-neighborhood TPI parameter).

param.name: declare_tpi_type_large
param.displayname: Declare large-neighborhood TPI type (optional, for warnings)

dialogReference.para: Optional. Declare what kind of TPI the existing large-neighborhood raster holds (Raw, Neighborhood standard deviation, DEM-scale standard deviation, or Percentile) when it is not stamped in the raster's metadata. The small and large TPIs are declared independently, so a classification may combine different TPI types at the two scales. Used only to warn about possibly incompatible units; the tool still runs even if a warning is shown. Leave blank if you do not want to declare it.
The pre-computed slope raster to classify, when using existing rasters (must match the other rasters' extent and cell size). Required when the classification system uses slope.

Optional. Declare the units (Degrees or Percent) of the existing slope raster when they are not stamped in its metadata. Used only to warn about possibly incompatible units; the tool still runs even if a warning is shown. Leave blank if you do not want to declare it.

scriptExample.title: Landform Classification example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Weiss 10-class landform from a DEM, small = 3-cell and large = 15-cell circular neighborhoods, followed by a run on existing rasters. The comment block lists every valid choice for the list-driven parameters; pass these strings EXACTLY as shown. The classification system listed is the bundled default -- any landform system you have created or edited in the Classification System Builder is equally valid (pass its name as shown in the Builder).
scriptExample.code:
import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages
# ---- valid options for the list-driven parameters ------------------------ # tpi_source: "Calculate TPI and Slope on-the-fly from DEM" # "Use Existing TPI and Slope Rasters" # system (bundled; user-created systems from the Classification System # Builder are also valid -- this list is not exhaustive): # "Weiss 10-Class Landform" # sm_shape / lg_shape: "Circle" | "Annulus" # sm_units / lg_units: "Cells" | "Meters" | "Kilometers" | "Feet" | "Miles" # tpi_type_small / tpi_type_large (on-the-fly; may differ from each other): # "Raw (elevation units)" # "Neighborhood standard deviation" # "Percentile" # elev_units: "Meters" | "Feet" # slope_method: "Planar" | "Geodesic" # slope_units: "Degrees" | "Percent" # declare_tpi_type_small / declare_tpi_type_large (existing mode, optional, # warnings only): # "Raw (elevation units)" # "Neighborhood standard deviation" # "DEM-scale standard deviation" # "Percentile" # declare_slope_units (existing mode, optional, warnings only): # "Degrees" | "Percent"
# 1) compute both TPIs and slope on the fly from a DEM arcpy.jenness.LandformClassification( tpi_source="Calculate TPI and Slope on-the-fly from DEM", in_raster="dem.tif", system="Weiss 10-Class Landform", out_raster="dem_Landform.tif", sm_shape="Circle", sm_outer=3, sm_inner=0, sm_units="Cells", lg_shape="Circle", lg_outer=15, lg_inner=0, lg_units="Cells", tpi_type_small="Neighborhood standard deviation", tpi_type_large="Neighborhood standard deviation", elev_units="Meters", slope_method="Planar", slope_units="Degrees", save_tpi_small="dem_TPI_sm.tif", save_tpi_large="dem_TPI_lg.tif", save_slope="dem_Slope.tif")
# 2) classify existing rasters as-is (the rasters saved above; the declare_* # parameters are optional -- rasters made by these tools carry their type # in their metadata already) arcpy.jenness.LandformClassification( tpi_source="Use Existing TPI and Slope Rasters", system="Weiss 10-Class Landform", out_raster="dem_Landform2.tif", in_tpi_small="dem_TPI_sm.tif", in_tpi_large="dem_TPI_lg.tif", in_slope="dem_Slope.tif", declare_tpi_type_small="Neighborhood standard deviation", declare_tpi_type_large="Neighborhood standard deviation", declare_slope_units="Degrees")

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Classify a DEM into landform categories from a small- and large-neighborhood TPI plus slope, using a saved classification system (e.g. Weiss 10-class); computed internally, no Spatial Analyst.
dataIdInfo.idAbs: Classifies a DEM into landform categories by combining the Topographic Position Index (elevation minus neighborhood mean; Weiss 2001) at a small and a large neighborhood with slope, driven by a reusable, saved classification system (thresholds, names, colors). Two-scale TPI distinguishes, for example, a local ridge inside a larger valley from an upland drainage. Neighborhoods (circle or annulus, cells or ground units) set the two scales; the system's units may be raw TPI (absolute, usually best for wildlife) or standardized (relative to variability). The two TPIs and slope are computed internally in numpy and classification is a single vectorized pass (lowest class value wins on overlap) with no Spatial Analyst or Con. Output is an integer class raster with a Value/Class_Name attribute table and color map. Bundled default: Weiss 10-class landform.
dataIdInfo.idCredit: Tool by Jeff Jenness, Jenness Enterprises (http://www.jennessent.com). Method: Weiss, A. 2001. Topographic Position and Landforms Analysis. ESRI Int'l User Conf. poster; Guisan, A., et al. 1999. Plant Ecology 143:107-122 (https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1009841519580). Suggested citation: Jenness, J. (2026). Landform Classification. Jenness Enterprises Wildlife Tools for ArcGIS Pro. http://www.jennessent.com.
